pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 9–11 years

- **Topic:** Wave Behaviour Vocabulary (refraction, absorption, reflection, scattering, amplitude, frequency, wavelength, echo, spectrum, angle of incidence, angle of reflection)

- **Standards — UK (DfE National Curriculum, Working Scientifically + KS2/KS3):** KS2 Working Scientifically requires pupils to 'read, spell and pronounce scientific vocabulary correctly.' The terms are drawn from KS2 Light (Y3/Y6: reflect) and Sound (Y4: vibration, volume, pitch) and, for the boundary/geometry terms (refraction, frequency, amplitude, wavelength, spectrum, angle of incidence, angle of reflection), from KS3 Physics 'Waves'. This record is the vocabulary spine that lets pupils APPLY those words when explaining how light and sound travel and interact with materials.

- **Standards — US (no NGSS vocabulary PE; CCSS-ELA anchor):** NGSS deliberately has no stand-alone vocabulary performance expectation — the Framework holds that terminology emerges from three-dimensional science practice, not isolated word-learning. The terms attach to the wave PEs 4-PS4-1/4-PS4-2 (elementary) and MS-PS4-2 (light/sound reflected, absorbed or transmitted through materials). The matching literacy standard is CCSS-ELA-LITERACY.L.5.6: 'acquire and use accurately grade-appropriate general academic and domain-specific words and phrases.'

- **Operational details:** This is a LANGUAGE topic, so the goal is precise, APPLIED use of a highly confusable term set — not rote definition. Teach each word against its nearest confusable neighbour, anchored on a single discriminator: does the wave BOUNCE back into the first medium (reflection), PASS THROUGH and bend into a new medium (refraction), spray off a rough surface in many directions (scattering), or get SOAKED IN and not returned (absorption)? Pin the three wave-property words to distinct visual features of ONE wave — amplitude = height, wavelength = distance peak-to-peak, frequency = how many pass per second — varying one at a time so they don't blur. Head off the known language traps: 'bending' (refraction) means a change from one straight path to another, not a curve; reflection is NOT only mirrors and refraction is NOT only glass blocks; and angle of incidence/reflection are measured from the NORMAL (the perpendicular), never from the surface. Every term should be used immediately in an explanation (bent straw = refraction; canyon echo = reflected sound; blue sky = scattering; prism rainbow = spectrum) per the DfE read/spell/USE requirement.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier B (transitional/early-formal), bridging from Tier A. The concrete terms (reflection, echo, absorption) are Tier A; the boundary/geometry terms (refraction, angle of incidence/reflection, spectrum) reach into early-formal. Mastery = correctly distinguishing reflection from refraction with the right definitions, using 'refraction' to explain the bent straw, and explaining an echo as reflected sound — applied, not merely recited. The quantitative law of reflection and v = fλ are deferred (Tier C, KS3/KS4).
bestPractices: Teach each term against its nearest confusable neighbour on ONE discriminator — bounce back (reflection) vs pass-through-and-bend (refraction) vs spray off a rough surface (scattering) vs soak in (absorption); remember air is usually the first medium.

Pin the three wave-property words to distinct visual features of a single wave (amplitude = height, wavelength = peak-to-peak, frequency = number per second) and vary ONE at a time so the terms don't blur together.
Confront the language traps explicitly: 'bending' in refraction is a change from one straight path to another (not a curve); reflection is not only mirrors; refraction is not only glass blocks.
Define angle of incidence and angle of reflection from the NORMAL (the perpendicular to the surface), not from the surface itself — the classic measurement error.

Use every term immediately in an explanation of a real phenomenon (bent straw = refraction, echo = reflected sound, blue sky = scattering, prism = spectrum), matching the DfE 'read, spell and USE scientific vocabulary' requirement.
Support correct spelling with word-part cues (re-FLECT = turn/bounce back; re-FRACT = break/bend through; ab-SORB = soak in) to reduce reflection–refraction confusion.
keyRepresentations: One incoming ray meeting a boundary with branching outcomes — bounce back (reflection), pass through and bend (refraction), soak in (absorption) — plus a rough-surface many-ray version (scattering).
A single labelled wave with amplitude, wavelength and frequency each called out on its own distinct feature.
A protractor drawn on the NORMAL showing angle of incidence = angle of reflection measured from the perpendicular.
Everyday exemplar cards each pinned to one term: bent straw (refraction), canyon echo (reflection of sound), blue sky (scattering), prism rainbow (spectrum).
commonMisconceptions: Swapping reflection and refraction — treating light that crosses into a new medium (refraction) as if it bounces off it (reflection).
Believing reflection is 'only mirrors' and refraction is 'only glass blocks', rather than every surface reflecting and any change of medium refracting.
Reading 'bending' (refraction) as light travelling in a CURVE instead of a change from one straight-line path to another.
Measuring the angle of incidence/reflection from the SURFACE rather than from the normal (the perpendicular).
Blurring amplitude, wavelength and frequency into a vague single 'size' of the wave instead of three distinct measurable features.
Not recognising absorption as an option (forcing every light–surface interaction into reflect or refract), and confusing scattering with plain mirror-like reflection.
Treating an 'echo' as a mysterious separate effect rather than simply reflected sound.

learn.summary: Applied vocabulary for wave behaviour (reflection, refraction, absorption, scattering, amplitude, wavelength, frequency, echo, spectrum, angle of incidence, angle of reflection) for ages 9–11. The teaching goal is precise, applied USE of a highly confusable term set, not rote definition: each word is taught against its nearest confusable neighbour on a single discriminator, and every term is immediately used to explain a real phenomenon (bent straw = refraction, echo = reflected sound, blue sky = scattering, prism = spectrum). Core discriminator: does the wave bounce back into the first medium (reflection), pass into a new medium and change direction at the boundary when it meets it at an angle (refraction), get sent off in many directions by a rough surface or by tiny particles such as those in air (scattering), or soak in and not return (absorption)? The three wave-property words pin to distinct features of one wave — amplitude = height from the middle (rest) line to a peak, wavelength = peak-to-peak distance, frequency = how many pass per second.

activities.title: One ray, four fates: send a ray at a boundary
feedback: If a learner labels the bent straw / crossing-into-glass case 'reflection', point out the ray entered the new medium and bent — that is refraction; reflection is when it bounces back without entering.
If a learner draws refraction as a curve, show that light travels straight within each medium and only changes direction AT the surface — straight, kink, straight.

If a learner thinks reflection is 'only mirrors' or refraction is 'only glass blocks', show that most surfaces reflect some light and that light can refract whenever it crosses at an angle into a material where it travels at a different speed (water, a lens, the surface of a swimming pool).
If absorption is overlooked, point to the black card: the light is soaked in and not sent back at all — a distinct option from reflect/refract.
activities.rationale: The whole difficulty is a confusable term set that separates best when each term is pinned to a distinct, changeable referent. Sending one ray at a boundary and watching its fate change ties each word to an observable outcome; flipping the same ray between glass and mirror directly targets the reflection↔refraction swap and the 'only mirrors / only glass' trap. A static glossary can assert these distinctions but a changeable ray lets the learner see the fate switch.
sourceClaims: Documented confusable-term misconceptions: pupils restrict reflection to mirrors and refraction to glass blocks; the 'bending' language for refraction misleads pupils into imagining a curve rather than a change from one straight-line path to another; the law of reflection (angle of incidence = angle of reflection) applies to all surfaces, not just plane mirrors.

The core discriminator between reflection and refraction is whether light BOUNCES off the second medium (reflection) or TRAVELS THROUGH it, bending (refraction); air is often the first medium. Students commonly conflate the two, treating light crossing into a new medium as being reflected.
learnerActions: Send a single light ray at a surface at an angle (not straight along the normal) and change what the surface is: a mirror, a block of glass or water, black card, and a rough/bumpy surface.

Watch and name the main outcome each time: mirror = bounces back off the surface (reflection); glass or water = most of the light passes through and bends at the surface (refraction), though a little is also reflected; black card = most of the light is soaked in and not returned (absorption); rough surface = sprays off in many directions (scattering).

Keep the SAME incoming ray and switch the surface from glass to mirror, and describe out loud how the ray changes from refracting to reflecting — the two most-confused words are two different fates of one ray.
Trace or draw the bent ray for refraction as two straight segments with a kink at the surface, NOT a curve.
State the first medium each time (usually air) and say which medium the ray crosses into.
activities.intendedInsight: Reflection, refraction, absorption and scattering are different things a wave can do when it meets a boundary; reflection (bounce back) and refraction (pass through and bend) are distinguished by whether the wave enters the new medium. Refraction is a change from one straight path to another with a kink at the boundary, not a curve.

activities.title: Measuring angles from the normal
feedback: If a learner measures from the surface, show that the standard definition uses the normal — redraw the perpendicular and measure from it.
Note that for these learners the point is correct measurement and definitions; the quantitative law of reflection (angle in = angle out as a numerical rule) and v = fλ come later.
activities.rationale: Measuring the angle from the surface instead of the normal is the classic measurement error flagged in reflection teaching; making the normal explicit and measuring from it addresses it directly. This measurement convention is a curriculum/pedagogy convention and is not restated word-for-word by any extracted source claim in this row.
learnerActions: On a reflection diagram, draw the normal — the line perpendicular to the surface at the point where the ray hits.
Measure the angle of incidence between the incoming ray and the normal, and the angle of reflection between the outgoing ray and the normal (for example with a protractor aligned to the normal).
Check that the two angles are measured from the normal, not from the surface, and compare them.
State in words: the angle of incidence and angle of reflection are both measured from the normal (the perpendicular).
activities.intendedInsight: Angles of incidence and reflection are measured from the normal (the perpendicular to the surface), never from the surface itself.

activities.title: One wave, three features: amplitude, wavelength, frequency
feedback: If a learner substitutes one term for another or says 'size', point to the feature each word names (height, peak spacing, waves per second) and change the amplitude to show that height changes while spacing and frequency stay fixed; when frequency changes, show that the wavelength changes with it, but they are still different measurements.
If a learner conflates loudness and pitch, link loudness to amplitude and pitch to frequency as separate features of a sound wave.
activities.rationale: Pinning each property word to its own visual feature and varying one at a time prevents the documented blur of amplitude/wavelength/frequency into a single notion of wave size, and connects to the known sound confusion between loudness and pitch.
sourceClaims: Wavelength is the distance between crests and frequency is the number of crests that pass a given point in one second (one cycle per second = one hertz).
Loudness/volume is linked to the size (amplitude) of the vibration, and pitch to frequency (how fast it vibrates); these are distinct wave features that pupils commonly conflate.
learnerActions: Look at a single labelled wave and identify amplitude = height, wavelength = distance from one peak to the next, frequency = how many waves pass per second.

Change one control at a time (for example an amplitude control, then a frequency control) and describe which feature changed and which word names it; notice that changing the amplitude leaves the peak spacing alone, but for a wave in the same material, raising the frequency makes the peaks closer together (shorter wavelength).
Say aloud a one-line distinction for each so they don't blur into a single vague 'size': amplitude is how tall, wavelength is how far apart the peaks are, frequency is how many per second.
Connect to sound: loudness/volume links to amplitude (size of the vibration) and pitch links to frequency (how fast it vibrates).
activities.intendedInsight: Amplitude, wavelength and frequency are three distinct, separately measurable features of one wave, not interchangeable words for its overall 'size'.

activities.title: Use the word to explain the phenomenon
feedback: If a learner names the echo but treats it as a mysterious separate effect, state plainly: an echo IS reflected sound — the same bounce-off-a-surface idea as a mirror reflection.

If a learner uses 'reflection' for the bent straw or 'refraction' for the echo, re-anchor each to its example — straw/lens = passes through and bends = refraction; mirror/echo = bounces back = reflection.
If a learner can only reach vague words like 'bends' or 'bounces', prompt for the precise term and the reason (which medium, bounce or pass-through).
activities.rationale: The curriculum requires pupils to read, spell and USE scientific vocabulary, and the assessment is explicitly applied (explain the bent straw, distinguish reflection from refraction, explain an echo). Using three contrasting contexts catches term swaps that a definition-recall task would miss, especially the reflection/refraction pair and whether 'echo' is named as reflected sound. A sort can check classification but does not itself elicit the spoken/written explanation, so explanation tasks are included.
sourceClaims: KS2 Working Scientifically requires pupils to read, spell and pronounce scientific vocabulary correctly; the wave-behaviour terms are drawn from KS2 Light & Sound and KS3 Physics 'Waves' (reflection, refraction, absorption, frequency, wavelength, amplitude, spectrum).

CCSS-ELA-LITERACY.L.5.6: acquire and use accurately grade-appropriate general academic and domain-specific words and phrases — the literacy standard matching applied scientific vocabulary, since NGSS has no stand-alone vocabulary PE.
learnerActions: For each everyday scene, say which term applies and why, in a full sentence: a straw looks bent where it enters a glass of water (refraction); you shout in a tunnel and hear your voice come back (echo — reflected sound); the sky looks blue (scattering); a prism makes a rainbow (spectrum).
Explain an echo as reflected sound, linking it to the same 'bounce off a surface' idea as light reflection (like seeing yourself in a mirror).

Explain the dull red jumper in shade: it absorbs most colours and reflects/scatters red, and in shade there is less light to reflect, so it looks duller (an illustrative case that depends on the actual material and lighting).
Sort a mix of scenarios into reflect / refract / absorb / scatter and justify each choice.
Use word-part cues to spell and separate the tricky pair: re-FLECT = bounce back, re-FRACT = break/bend through, ab-SORB = soak in.
activities.intendedInsight: Each wave term earns its keep by explaining a real phenomenon; mastery is applying the right word in context, keeping reflection distinct from refraction, and recognising an echo as simply reflected sound.

constraints: This is a LANGUAGE topic: the goal is precise, applied use of a confusable term set, not rote definition — every term should be used to explain a real phenomenon.

Teach each term against its nearest confusable neighbour on ONE discriminator (bounce back vs pass-through-and-bend vs sent off in many directions by a rough surface or tiny particles vs soak in); remember air is usually the first medium.
Refraction 'bending' is a change from one straight path to another with a kink at the boundary, not a curve; draw it as straight segments with a kink.

Angles of incidence and reflection are measured from the normal (the perpendicular), never from the surface; reflection off a mirror returns at an equal angle from the normal, not necessarily straight back along the incoming path.

Vary only one feature at a time where possible so amplitude, wavelength and frequency do not blur into a vague single 'size': amplitude can be changed on its own, but for a wave travelling in the same medium, changing the frequency also changes the wavelength (higher frequency, shorter wavelength).
The quantitative law of reflection (angle in = angle out as a numerical rule) and v = fλ are deferred to later stages (KS3/KS4); keep the focus on correct terms and measurement conventions.

A look-up reference or glossary pairing each term with its exemplar is a useful companion that can assert distinctions statically; for a confusable set, learners also benefit from seeing a ray's fate change and features vary, so a reference should support rather than replace applied discrimination (neither is a universal requirement).

Matching, sorting, multiple-choice and fill-the-blank response formats can assess the applied vocabulary and check classification, but do not by themselves build the visual discrimination or elicit an explanation; pair them with observation and spoken/written reasoning.
Recognition-only responses (choosing a label) do not elicit independent construction of an explanation; include tasks where the learner states the term AND the reason.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Several cited sources are marked unverified in the source row (DfE National Curriculum, Texas Gateway, CCSS-ELA); the IOPSpark, NASA and Explorify claims are marked verified. Citations support the stated teaching principles but do not establish that any specific activity here has been empirically tested or is comparatively more effective.

The from-the-normal measurement convention in the 'Measuring angles from the normal' activity is a curriculum/pedagogy convention; no extracted sources[].claim in this row states the surface-vs-normal measurement error directly, so that activity's sourceClaims is left empty rather than citing a topic-level claim.

The original material in places implied a static glossary 'cannot' teach confusable sets and that a changeable ray is uniquely required; this has been softened to a scoped affordance claim (changeable referents let learners observe fate/feature changes) without asserting universal necessity.

The mirror case in activity 1 was reworded from 'bounces straight back' to 'bounces back off the surface' to avoid implying retroreflection, keeping it consistent with the equal-angle-from-the-normal activity.

The 'dull red jumper in shade' explanation combines absorption/reflection of colour with reduced illumination in shade; this is reasonable at this level but depends on the actual material and lighting, so it is presented as an illustrative case, not an absolute outcome.

probeDeeper: In the bent-straw case, is the light bouncing back, or passing through and changing direction? Which word is that?
What is an echo actually made of — how is it like seeing yourself in a mirror?
The straw looks bent, but does the light travel in a curve or in straight lines with a kink at the water's surface? Which word describes it?
assess.correctAnswer: The bent straw = refraction (light changes direction and speed crossing the water-air boundary). The voice coming back = an echo, which is reflection of sound off the tunnel wall. The dull red jumper = it absorbs most colours and reflects/scatters red, and in shade there is less light to reflect. Terms are USED correctly and reflection is kept distinct from refraction.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reflection/refraction swapped: uses 'reflection' for the bent straw or 'refraction' for the echo
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reflection = bounces back off a surface; refraction = passes through and changes direction at a boundary; anchor each to its example (mirror/echo versus straw/lens).
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Applies the wrong term to bending-across-a-boundary versus bouncing-back

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Bending' misread as a curve: thinks refraction makes light follow a curved path
errorPatterns.nextMove: Refraction is a change of direction AT the boundary — straight in each medium, a kink at the surface, not a curve.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Describes the refracted ray as curving, rather than as a straight path that changes direction at the boundary

errorPatterns.pattern: Echo as a mystery, not reflected sound: names the echo but can't connect it to reflection
errorPatterns.nextMove: An echo IS reflected sound — the same 'bounce off a surface' idea as light reflection.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Calls it an echo but treats it as a separate phenomenon, not sound bouncing off a surface

errorPatterns.pattern: Amplitude/frequency/wavelength blurred into 'size': uses one for another or a vague 'how big'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Pin each term to one feature — amplitude = height, wavelength = distance between peaks, frequency = how many per second.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Substitutes amplitude for frequency or wavelength, or uses 'size' to cover all three

responseLevels.gap: Swaps reflection and refraction, or can't reach for any correct term in context (uses only vague 'bends'/'bounces').
responseLevels.full: Applies each term accurately across the three contexts, keeps reflection distinct from refraction, names the echo as reflected sound, and pins amplitude/wavelength/frequency to distinct features.
responseLevels.partial: Uses some terms correctly but muddles the reflection/refraction pair or treats echo/absorption loosely; amplitude/frequency/wavelength blur into 'size'.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here are three things happening: a straw looks bent where it enters a glass of water; you shout in a tunnel and hear your voice come back a moment later; and a red jumper looks dull in the shade. Tell me what's happening in each, using the right wave words — you might need reflection, refraction, absorption, scattering, echo. Explain your choices.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: These terms are notoriously confused — reflection versus refraction, 'bending' misread as a curve, echo seen as mysterious rather than reflected sound. Giving three contexts and listening for which word the child reaches for catches swaps that a definition-recall task would miss, especially the reflection/refraction pair and whether 'echo' is named as reflected sound.
